571.event_title: Fridtjof Nansen creates the Nansen passport for stateless refugees
571.event: After the Soviet government revoked the citizenship of Russians living abroad in 1921, hundreds of thousands of refugees from the Russian civil war were left without any state that would issue them papers. Fridtjof Nansen, the Norwegian explorer serving as the League of Nations' first High Commissioner for Refugees, convened an intergovernmental conference in Geneva in July 1922 that agreed on an identity certificate for these stateless people. The Nansen passport was later extended to Armenian and other refugees, roughly 450,000 were issued, and Nansen received the 1922 Nobel Peace Prize for his refugee and relief work.
571.explanation: A single act of considerate regard for people who belonged nowhere gave them back the ordinary ability to travel, work and live among nations.
571.tie_back: The kural says the world keeps going because of the great beauty of kindly regard, and the Nansen passport shows that regard quite literally reopening the world's doors to people the world had shut out.
571._accuracy_note: A strong case of kindly regard keeping the world's ordinary life going for those cut off from it; the kural's claim is universal, while this is one notable instance.

572.event_title: Clara Barton founds the American Red Cross
572.event: Clara Barton, who had nursed and supplied soldiers during the American Civil War and later ran an office that traced missing soldiers, learned of the European Red Cross movement in Switzerland in 1869 and worked with it during the Franco-Prussian War. On 21 May 1881 she founded the American Red Cross in Washington, D.C., and in 1882 the United States ratified the Geneva Convention. She led the organisation for 23 years, and her push for peacetime disaster relief led the International Red Cross Conference to adopt the so-called American Amendment in 1884.
572.explanation: Barton made organised compassion a permanent part of everyday national life, so that help after floods, fires and wars no longer depended on chance.
572.tie_back: The kural says the ordinary business of the world runs on kindly regard, and Barton's Red Cross turned that regard into an institution that ordinary communities still rely on in every disaster.
572._accuracy_note: Illustrates the positive half of the kural, that the world's dealings rest on kindness; it does not show the kural's sharper point that the unkind are a burden on the earth.

573.event_title: Yehudi Menuhin and Benjamin Britten play for the survivors of Bergen-Belsen
573.event: A few months after British troops liberated the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, the violinist Yehudi Menuhin made a short tour of displaced persons' camps in Germany, with the composer Benjamin Britten as his pianist. On 27 July 1945 they gave two concerts at Belsen for survivors who were still living there. Among the listeners was the cellist Anita Lasker, who had survived Auschwitz and Belsen.
573.explanation: Two celebrated musicians chose to bring their art to people who had suffered terribly, joining musical skill to human compassion.
573.tie_back: The kural asks what use a melody is if it does not fit the song, and what use an eye is without kindness; at Belsen, music was given its fitting purpose by being joined to compassion for those who heard it.
573._accuracy_note: Next-best: the kural uses music only as a simile for an eye without kindness, and this event matches music with compassion rather than illustrating the eye directly.

574.event_title: Elizabeth Fry visits the women prisoners of Newgate
574.event: Early in 1813 a friend urged Elizabeth Fry, a Quaker minister, to visit the women's side of Newgate Prison, and she went in although the jailer warned her that the prisoners were dangerous. She found several hundred women and their children crowded into a few rooms, some sleeping on the floor. Fry kept returning, started a school for the prisoners' children, and with the prisoners and authorities introduced a matron, classification, education and paid sewing work, founding a Ladies' Association for Newgate in 1817.
574.explanation: Many officials had looked at Newgate for years; Fry was among the first to look at its women with real concern, and her measured, practical kindness changed prison practice in Britain.
574.tie_back: The kural says eyes without kindly regard in due measure only seem to be present; the officials' eyes had seen Newgate without effect, while Fry's regard, combined with order and discipline, actually did good.
574._accuracy_note: Fits the idea that eyes are useful only when they carry measured kindness; the contrast with the jailers who looked but did nothing is implied rather than documented in detail.

575.event_title: Audrey Hepburn's UNICEF mission to famine-struck Somalia
575.event: Audrey Hepburn, the film star, served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador for a token salary of one dollar a year and had already visited Ethiopia, Sudan and Bangladesh for the agency. In 1992 she spent several days flying around central Somalia during the famine, visiting a feeding centre at Baidoa where starving children were being cared for. She was already seriously ill, underwent surgery in November 1992, and died in January 1993.
575.explanation: In her last working year, one of the world's most admired faces chose to be seen looking with compassion at suffering that much of the world had ignored.
575.tie_back: The kural calls kindly regard the jewel of the eye, and Hepburn is remembered less for her famous looks than for the compassionate gaze she turned on Somalia's children.
575._accuracy_note: A good image of kindness as the true ornament of a famously beautiful person; the kural's jewel-versus-sore contrast is only implicitly present.

576.event_title: The Evian Conference on refugees from Nazi Germany
576.event: At President Franklin Roosevelt's initiative, delegates from 32 countries and a number of aid organisations met for nine days at Evian on Lake Geneva to discuss Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany and annexed Austria. Nearly all the governments represented declined to open their doors to more refugees, and the Dominican Republic was the only participant that offered to accept significant additional numbers. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum concludes that the conference had very little impact on the refugees' plight.
576.explanation: The conference is remembered as a moment when the world's governments looked directly at people in danger and, apart from rare exceptions, did not act.
576.tie_back: The kural says those who have eyes but never look kindly are like trees rooted in the soil, having the form of seeing without the feeling, which is what most delegations at Evian displayed.
576._accuracy_note: A clear historical case of people who saw suffering without kindly response; it concerns governments rather than individuals, and the conference took place before the full scale of later persecution was known.

577.event_title: Bartolome de las Casas gives up his encomienda in Cuba
577.event: Bartolome de las Casas had come to the Caribbean as a settler, served as a chaplain in the Spanish conquest of Cuba, and was granted land and Indigenous labourers under the encomienda system. Influenced by Dominican friars who denounced the treatment of the Indigenous people, he renounced his encomienda and freed the people assigned to him around 1514, and began preaching that other colonists should do the same. When his preaching in Cuba had little effect he went to Spain to plead the case at court, and he spent the rest of his long life defending the Indigenous peoples of the Americas.
577.explanation: Las Casas had lived among the same suffering for years before he truly saw it; once he did, he could not look away for the rest of his life.
577.tie_back: The kural says those without kindly regard are really eyeless and those who truly have eyes are never without it, and Las Casas's turning point was the moment his sight became real sight.
577._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of moral sight replacing mere seeing; sources differ on the exact year and on which sermon prompted the change.

578.event_title: George Washington's Newburgh Address to his discontented officers
578.event: Near the end of the American Revolutionary War, Continental Army officers who had gone months or years without pay or promised pensions circulated an anonymous address threatening to defy Congress. George Washington forbade the meeting they had called and summoned the officers himself on 15 March 1783, where he read a speech that sympathised with their grievances but condemned the methods being proposed. The next day the officers passed a unanimous resolution commending Washington, the threatened mutiny ended, and Washington kept pressing Congress until the officers were granted five years' full pay.
578.explanation: Washington showed real understanding of his officers' hardship without letting that sympathy override his duty to uphold civilian authority.
578.tie_back: The kural says the world belongs to those who can show kindly regard without letting their duty be damaged, and at Newburgh Washington's sympathy for his men and his duty to the republic stood side by side.
578._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural's balance of kindness and duty; the kural speaks of a king's justice, here applied to a commander and his officers.

579.event_title: J. R. Jayewardene urges forgiveness of Japan at the San Francisco Peace Conference
579.event: At the conference called to make peace with Japan after the Second World War, Ceylon's finance minister J. R. Jayewardene addressed the delegates in the War Memorial Opera House. Citing the Buddha's teaching that hatred is ended not by hatred but by love, he argued that Japan should be allowed to rejoin the community of nations as a free country, and Ceylon renounced its claim to reparations. Japanese leaders have repeatedly acknowledged the speech in the decades since.
579.explanation: A country that had suffered wartime attack chose to answer its former enemy with forbearance rather than retribution.
579.tie_back: The kural calls it the highest virtue to show kindly regard and patiently bear with even those who have hurt us, and Ceylon's stand at San Francisco extended that regard to a former enemy.
579._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's call to bear with those who harmed us; the speech's exact influence on other delegations is described differently by different sources.

580.event_title: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson renew their friendship
580.place: Quincy, Massachusetts, and Monticello, Virginia, United States
580.event: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, partners in the American Revolution, became bitter political opponents, and after Jefferson defeated Adams in the 1800 presidential election the two men stopped writing to each other. Their mutual friend Benjamin Rush spent years urging them to make peace, and in 1812 Adams wrote to Jefferson and Jefferson replied. They then corresponded until both died on 4 July 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.
580.explanation: Two men who had wounded each other deeply in public life chose to set the injuries aside and value the friendship above them.
580.tie_back: The kural praises those who, for the sake of courtesy and friendship, will swallow even a bitter injury from a friend and stay at peace with him, as Adams and Jefferson did for the last fourteen years of their lives.
580._accuracy_note: A well-documented case of friends accepting past hurts to keep the friendship; the kural's image of knowingly drinking poison from a friend is far more extreme than anything here.
